articles.title: An agent that pays for its own timestamps: x402 on a CPU-mined coin
articles.excerpt: Every night at 23:41 an agent we run, on OpenClaw on a Mac mini, makes a list of the SHA-256 of every file in its notes, takes the SHA-256 of that list and stamps it into a blockchain. It pays for the…
articles.body: Every night at 23:41 an agent we run, on OpenClaw on a Mac mini, makes a list of the SHA-256 of every file in its notes, takes the SHA-256 of that list and stamps it into a blockchain. It pays for the stamp itself. It has no card and no USDC: it pays in NORTH, the coin of TrueNorth, which ordinary processors mine. This post shows how that works, what it costs, what went wrong, and when you should use something else. What a stamp is for A stamp proves that some data existed no later than a given block. For an agent that means: these were its notes on that night, and nobody changed them afterwards without it showing. The same goes for logs, model outputs or release files. Only the SHA-256 leaves the machine, never the file.

The redirect rules are built from it, so every mistake in the map becomes a live mistake on launch day. We move sites between platforms (Webflow, Shopify, WordPress, custom code), and we check the map before anything goes live. This post covers the three kinds of mistakes we look for, with real output from redirect-map-check , the free, open-source checker we built for it: Old URLs the map leaves out Rows that send a URL to the wrong page Rows that contradict each other All examples come from the tool's demo shop, Harbor & Pine. articles.title: SpaceX Starship debris becomes art in Ashley Zelinskie's 'The Weight of Space' (video, photos)
articles.excerpt: Explore Ashley Zelinskie's 'The Weight of Space' Monuments in marble, Ejecta prints, Launch Sequence sculptures and interactive Crowded Sky at Heft Gallery in New York City.
articles.body: When a SpaceX Starship broke apart over Turks and Caicos in Jan. 2025, pieces of its heat shield washed ashore. Some of that material now hangs on a gallery wall in New York City, embedded in artist Ashley Zelinskie's print of the very explosion it survived. Look closely at the print and you can see little flakes on the surface. Some of Zelinskie's friends vacationing on the islands had come across pieces of heat-shield tile. "I think you might want these," Zelinskie recalled one friend telling her. She did. The Brooklyn-based artist ground the fragments into dust and worked them into the print. Ashley Zelinskie incorporated dust from recovered SpaceX Starship heat-shield tiles into this print of the vehicle breaking apart over Turks and Caicos.

articles.excerpt: The FCC has given SpaceX approval to deploy one million of its Starmind AI data-center satellites in orbit, a move that could transform the landscape of the final frontier.
articles.body: Earth orbit could get a lot more crowded in the coming years. The U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) just granted SpaceX approval to deploy one million of its Starmind AI data-center satellites in orbit. "This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said today (Nov. 25) in a statement announcing the approval. AI has become central to SpaceX's business plans and identity over the past year or so.
